```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(simdfuse)
set.seed(20260114)
ulp <- function(got, want) {
  ok <- is.finite(want) & want != 0 & is.finite(got)
  max(abs(got[ok] - want[ok]) / 2^(floor(log2(abs(want[ok]))) - 52))
}
```

A faster answer that is quietly a different answer is not a faster answer. This
page sets out exactly what `simdfuse` promises, what it does not, and where it
deliberately disagrees with base R. The figures below are computed when this
vignette is built, on your machine.

## Elementwise arithmetic is bit-identical

In the default `math = "accurate"` mode, every elementwise expression returns
the same bits as base R, with one exception described below. Elementary
functions are routed through the same platform `libm` that R calls, one lane at
a time; `pnorm`, `dnorm`, `plogis` and `qlogis` call R's own routines rather
than being rebuilt from `erfc`.

```{r}
x <- runif(1e5, 0.1, 10); y <- runif(1e5, -5, 5); mu <- 2.5; s <- 1.25
c(arith   = identical(sf(x * y - 2.5), x * y - 2.5),
  expo    = identical(sf(exp(y)), exp(y)),
  logs    = identical(sf(log(x, 2)), log(x, 2)),
  powers  = identical(sf(x^3 - y^2), x^3 - y^2),
  dist    = identical(sf(dnorm(y, mu, s)), dnorm(y, mu, s)),
  ifelses = identical(sf(ifelse(x > y, x, y)), ifelse(x > y, x, y)))
```

## The exception: `sqrt` on a platform whose `libm` is not correctly rounded

`sqrt` is the one function simdfuse does not take from `libm`. Every backend
uses the hardware square root -- `sqrtsd`, `vsqrtpd`, `fsqrt` -- which IEEE 754
requires to be correctly rounded. Base R reaches `sqrt` through a function
pointer in its internal `math1()`, so it always gets the C library routine, and
not every C library returns the correctly rounded value.

```{r}
c(bit_identical = identical(sf(sqrt(x)), sqrt(x)),
  disagreements = sum(sf(sqrt(x)) != sqrt(x)))
```

On glibc and on Apple's `libm` that is `TRUE` and `0`. On R 4.5.2 for Windows
it is `FALSE`, with about one argument in two thousand differing by exactly one
ulp. In every case examined there, the true root lay within 2e-4 of the
midpoint between two adjacent doubles -- the signature of a result computed to
extended precision and then rounded a second time -- and comparing `r^2` with
`x` in exact arithmetic showed the hardware value to be the nearer of the two.
So simdfuse is the more accurate of the pair on that platform, and the price is
that it is not bit-identical to base R there. The package's test suite asserts
this explicitly rather than relaxing to a tolerance: a differing element is
accepted only where our value is provably the nearer root.

Three details took real care and are worth knowing about:

* **`x^k`.** R's arithmetic special-cases only `y == 2`, turning it into `x * x`,
  and otherwise calls `pow()`. Replacing `x^3` with repeated squaring would be
  faster and would differ in the last bit, so in accurate mode it is not done.
* **Fused multiply-add.** Contracting `a*b + c` into one instruction removes a
  rounding step. It is therefore emitted only in `fast` mode.
* **`NA` versus `NaN`.** R distinguishes them by the payload bits of a quiet
  `NaN`. Comparisons, the logical operators and `ifelse()` produce R's `NA`;
  `pmin`/`pmax` propagate missingness by adding their operands, exactly as base
  R does, so the payload survives.

```{r}
g <- expand.grid(a = c(1, 0, NA), b = c(1, 0, NA))
p <- g$a; q <- g$b
lp <- as.logical(p); lq <- as.logical(q)
identical(sf(p & q), lp & lq) && identical(sf(p | q), lp | lq)
```

## The fast mode, and what it costs

`math = "fast"` offers SIMD polynomial `exp()` and `log()` and allows
multiply-add contraction. The error is bounded and measured, not hoped for:

```{r}
xe <- runif(2e5, -700, 700)
xl <- 10^runif(2e5, -300, 300)
c(exp_ulp = ulp(sf(exp(xe), math = "fast"), exp(xe)),
  log_ulp = ulp(sf(log(xl), math = "fast"), log(xl)))
```

One to three units in the last place across the full representable range,
subnormal inputs included. The boundary behaviour -- overflow to `Inf`,
underflow to zero, `NaN` and the infinities -- is exact.

The one deviation to know about: the polynomials destroy the payload that
distinguishes `NA` from `NaN`, so `exp(NA)` returns `NaN` in fast mode.
`is.na()` is `TRUE` either way, so only code that separates the two is affected.

```{r}
na <- c(NA_real_, 1)
c(fast = is.nan(sf(exp(na), math = "fast"))[1],
  accurate = is.nan(sf(exp(na), math = "accurate"))[1])
```

### Fast mode is not always faster, so it is not always taken

A vectorised polynomial costs a fixed number of operations per vector no matter
how wide that vector is, so it only pays for itself once there are enough lanes
to spread the cost over. Below that it loses to the system `libm`, and the
crossover is not a property of the lane count alone -- it also depends on how
good the local `libm` is. Measured against glibc, the polynomial `log()` runs at
0.54x of `libm` on the scalar backend, 0.74x on SSE2, 1.55x on AVX2 and 3.08x on
AVX-512; measured against Apple's `libm` on two-lane NEON, polynomial `exp()`
wins at 1.71x where polynomial `log()` loses at 0.80x. The same lane count, the
same package, opposite answers.

So the choice is per function and per machine, and it is measured rather than
predicted. `sf_tune()` times both ways and sets `fast_exp` and `fast_log`
accordingly; they can also be set by hand.

```{r}
unlist(sf_options()[c("fast_exp", "fast_log")])
```

When one of them is off, `math = "fast"` falls back to the same `libm` call
`math = "accurate"` makes, which means fast mode is then *bit-identical to base
R* for that function -- the `NA`-versus-`NaN` deviation above included. This is
the one place where a `simdfuse` result depends on the host rather than only on
the inputs, which is why it is reported rather than hidden:

```{r}
sf_info()[c("isa", "lanes")]
```

## Reductions: deterministic in the thread count

A parallel sum normally depends on how the work was divided, so the same code
gives different last bits on a laptop and on a cluster node. `simdfuse` cuts
work into tasks whose boundaries depend only on `n`, never on the thread count,
and combines task partials serially in index order in extended precision. The
answer is therefore the same on one thread and on sixty:

```{r}
z <- rnorm(1e6) * 10^runif(1e6, -8, 8)   # a deliberately brutal summation
vals <- vapply(1:4, function(k) sf_sum(quote(z), threads = k), 0)
length(unique(vals)) == 1L
```

This is a stronger guarantee than `OpenMP`'s `reduction(+:)` clause can offer.
What it is *not* is bit-identity with `sum()`: base R accumulates sequentially
in long double, while this is blocked summation, which is usually the more
accurate of the two but is a different operation.

```{r}
c(simdfuse = sf_sum(quote(z)), base = sum(z))
```

Determinism holds across thread counts at a fixed block size and instruction
set. It does not hold across *different* block sizes or instruction sets, since
both change how values are grouped before they are added. For results that must
match across heterogeneous machines, pin both:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sf_options(isa = "avx2", block = 128L)
```

## Where simdfuse deliberately disagrees with base R

`x %% y` is computed in R as `x - floor(x/y) * y`, which carries no information
once `|x/y|` exceeds `1/eps`; R notices and warns. `simdfuse` routes through
`fmod()`, which is exact by definition.

```{r}
r_value  <- withCallingHandlers(1e300 %% 7,
              warning = function(w) invokeRestart("muffleWarning"))
v <- c(1e300, 1e300); sf_value <- sf(v %% 7)[1]

digits <- as.numeric(strsplit(format(1e300, scientific = FALSE), "")[[1]])
exact <- 0; for (d in digits) exact <- (exact * 10 + d) %% 7

c(base_R = r_value, simdfuse = sf_value, exact = exact)
```

Below that threshold the two agree bit for bit. The same choice removes a
subtler problem: computing the remainder the direct way made the AVX2 kernel
disagree with the SSE2 kernel by one unit in the last place, because the
compiler contracted the multiply-subtract on one and not the other. Answers
that depend on which CPU you happen to be running on are a worse failure than
answers that differ from base R for a documented reason, so every backend is
checked against every other in the test suite.

`sf_stencil()` also differs from `stats::filter()` by convention rather than by
accident: `weights[1]` multiplies the earliest element of the window, so
`c(-1/2, 0, 1/2)` is a centred first difference. `filter()` takes the weights
in the reverse order.

## Summary

| | guarantee |
|---|---|
| elementwise, `math = "accurate"` | bit-identical to base R |
| `sqrt` | correctly rounded; bit-identical to base R wherever the platform `libm` is also correctly rounded |
| elementwise, `math = "fast"` | `exp` within 2 ulp, `log` within 4 ulp; `NA` becomes `NaN`. Per-function, and only where measurement showed the polynomial wins -- otherwise bit-identical to base R |
| reductions | identical across thread counts; not bit-identical to `sum()` |
| reductions across block size or instruction set | not guaranteed; pin both if it matters |
| `sf_scan(parallel = FALSE)` | identical to `cumsum`, `cummax`, `cummin` |
| `sf_scan(parallel = TRUE)` | identical for `max` and `min`; reassociated for `sum` and `prod` |
| `%%`, `%/%` | identical where base R is reliable, exact beyond that |
